contexts.text: A wall plastered with what is unfit () = fiction appearing as truth. AC 7553:3.
Such are but plasterers of the wall.
They live in... huts of rushes and reeds plastered over with lime.
The houses were built of bricks, with beams between, and plastered over.
The light, by its flickering on the plastered walls, presented birds of night.
They are like plastered walls, the plastering beautifully coloured, within which fly birds of night.
The walls of (Melancthon's) room appeared plastered with lime.
The former plastering and emptiness then returned.
Concerning Spirits who pervert holy things; [represented] by a plastering of what is unfit.
They as it were plaster over holy things, and thus bring them to the perception of man.
Such dwell within a wall... white, as if of plastered gypsum, with beautiful sculptures made of the gypsum.
A chamber plastered within with something snowy; built of brick work, but plastered... There was profanity there.
A large continuous building... of stone plastered with lime of a grey colour... Temples also of plastered stone...
Plastering () = application, and the derivative apparent confirmation.
Those who plaster what is unfit () = those who confirm falsities, so that outwardly they appear like truths.
The plastering of what is unfit () = the confirmation of falsity by means of fallacies, through which falsity appears like truth. Coro 34:3.
